hints: Look at the products, one is a radical with a dot on carbon and the other gains the H. Think about how the shared pair in the C-H bond must have split to give this result.
walkthrough:
Picture what happens to the shared electrons**
Think of the $\text{C-H}$ bond as one pair of electrons shared between C and H. In this step the H leaves the carbon and joins $\text{NO}_2$, while the carbon is left with an unpaired electron as $\text{CH}_3\dot{\text{C}}\text{=O}$. That tells you each fragment keeps one electron from the pair.
Final answer: This reaction involves homolytic fission of the single covalent bond between a hydrogen atom and a carbon atom in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$.

hints: Count outer shell electrons first. N brings 5, each O brings 6, H brings 1. Remember $\text{NO}_2$ has one unpaired electron on N, while in $\text{HNO}_2$ all electrons are paired because H adds one more electron.
walkthrough:
Build NO2 with its odd electron**
Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons and each oxygen has 6. Join N to each O with a covalent bond. After sharing, you will find N still has one single unpaired electron left over. That is why $\text{NO}_2$ is a radical. Each O keeps two lone pairs plus the bonding pairs to complete its octet.

Add H to make HNO2 with all paired**
Now the H atom brings one electron to bond to one O atom to give $\text{H-O-N=O}$. That extra electron pairs up the previously unpaired electron on N, so N now has a full lone pair. In your diagram show H with its pair shared to O, N with one lone pair, one $\text{N-O}$ single bond and one $\text{N=O}$ double bond, and complete octets on both O atoms.

Final answer: $\text{NO}_2$: N central bonded to two O atoms, one unpaired electron on N, each O has two lone pairs plus bonding electrons to complete octet. $\text{HNO}_2$: $\text{H-O-N=O}$, H bonded to O, N bonded to two O atoms with one lone pair on N, all electrons paired.

hints: Count regions of electron density around N in $\text{HNO}_2$. Include both bonding pairs to the two O atoms and the lone pair on N, then recall how a lone pair squeezes the ideal trigonal planar angle.
walkthrough:
Apply VSEPR at nitrogen**
Around N in $\text{HNO}_2$ you have two $\text{N-O}$ bonding regions plus one lone pair, so three electron domains in total. The basic shape is trigonal planar with an ideal $120^{\circ}$ angle. Because a lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, it squeezes the $\text{O-N-O}$ angle slightly below $120^{\circ}$, so any value around $115-120^{\circ}$ is accepted.

hints: Start from the rate equation $\text{rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}][\text{NO}_2]$ and rearrange in your head to make $k$ the subject before putting numbers in.
Think about how units combine. Rate has $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$ and each concentration has $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, so work out what units $k$ must have to balance the equation.
walkthrough:
Rearrange and substitute**
You know $\text{rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}][\text{NO}_2]$, so $$k = \frac{\text{rate}}{[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}][\text{NO}_2]}$$ Put in the numbers: $$k = \frac{1.53 \times 10^{-4}}{(0.200)(0.200)} = \frac{1.53 \times 10^{-4}}{0.0400} = 3.825 \times 10^{-3}$$

Work out the units carefully**
Rearrange units in the same way: $$\text{units of } k = \frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})} = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}\text{s}^{-1}$$ This is exactly what you expect for an overall second order rate constant. So $k = 3.83 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}\text{s}^{-1}$.

hints: Recall which order is special for half-life. Only one order gives a constant half-life independent of starting concentration, so check the overall order from the rate equation in (b).
walkthrough:
Link order to half-life behaviour**
From (b), $\text{rate} = k[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}][\text{NO}_2]$, first order in each reactant, so overall order = 2. A constant half-life is a unique fingerprint of first order kinetics only. For second order, half-life gets longer as concentration falls, so the $[\text{NO}_2]$ against time plot will not show a constant half-life.

Final answer: prediction: no constant half-life
explanation: overall second order reaction, only first order reactions have constant half-life.

hints: The rate equation $\text{rate} = k_1[\text{NO}_2]$ is first order, so half-life is constant. Recall the A Level expression linking $t_{1/2}$ to $k$ using $\ln 2$.
walkthrough:
Use the first order half-life expression**
For first order, $$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k_1} = \frac{0.693}{0.0848}$$ Calculate: $$t_{1/2} = 8.17 \text{ s}$$ No concentration data is needed because $t_{1/2}$ is independent of concentration for first order.

hints: Picture gases meeting a solid surface. What is the name of the step where $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ stick onto the catalyst surface?
Once stuck, think about what happens to bonds inside the reactant molecules and what must happen for the product to free up the surface again.
walkthrough:
Adsorption onto the surface**
Imagine $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ diffusing to the metal surface in the converter. They form weak bonds to the surface atoms, this is adsorption. This holds them close together in the correct orientation and concentrates them.

Weakening bonds and releasing products**
Interaction with the surface weakens bonds within the reactant molecules, providing an alternative route of lower activation energy. After reaction, the products detach, this is desorption, leaving the surface free for fresh reactants. The catalyst is unchanged.

Final answer: Reactants are adsorbed onto the catalyst surface.
Bonds within reactant molecules are weakened, lowering activation energy.
Products are desorbed from the catalyst surface.
